foundation.statement: Architecture practices rarely choose poorly. They choose reactively, without a coherent framework, and then live with the consequences compounding across years. The real problem is structural, not technical.

hero.heading: A clearer view of how your practice really works.
hero.lede: I’m Allister Lewis, an architect and technology strategist. I founded ADDD to help architecture leaders understand what is really holding their practice back—across technology, workflows, information, costs and decision-making.

perspective.heading: What Allister sees
perspective.lede: An external eye finds what internal teams have learned to live with.

tiles.text: Every practice has them. Manual steps inserted between tools. Data re-entered because systems do not talk. Email used as workflow because nothing else fits. These are not inefficiencies. They are invisible infrastructure. No one reports them because everyone assumes they are normal. An external review makes them visible and shows what becomes possible when they are removed.
tiles.title: Workarounds that became the system

tiles.text: One team picks software for speed. Another chooses based on cost. A third inherits legacy systems no one wants to replace. Each decision made sense at the time. Together they create governance gaps, duplicated data, conflicting workflows and costs that climb without visibility. The problem is not the tools. It is the absence of a framework that connects them.
tiles.title: Fragmented choices that compound into risk

tiles.text: Partners assume BIM is embedded. Project directors know it is partial. Teams use workarounds leadership has never seen. Investment in training does not translate to adoption. What gets reported upwards and what happens on projects are often two different stories. Closing that gap is where real change begins.
tiles.title: The gap between what leadership believes and what actually happens

hero.heading: Software & Licensing Audit
hero.lede: A complete account of what your practice pays for and what it actually uses. Every seat, every renewal date, every overlapping subscription—set against real usage, so renewal conversations start from evidence instead of habit. ADDD assesses software cost and licensing as part of the wider technology strategy, usually within a Technology Blueprint.

method.heading: How it works
method.lede: Four stages across roughly four weeks. The heaviest lift is gathering records at the start; after that the work sits with us until the readout.

steps.label: Stage one
steps.text: Invoices, licence agreements, admin consoles and expense lines. We build one register of every product, contract term, renewal date and seat count.
steps.title: Collect the records

steps.label: Stage two
steps.text: Allocated seats are compared against actual activity. Dormant licences, duplicated products and users holding access they no longer need are identified by name.
steps.title: Match seats to use

steps.label: Stage three
steps.text: Pricing, tiers and bundling are checked against how comparable products are sold. This is where consolidation and renegotiation opportunities surface.
steps.title: Test the commercial position

steps.label: Stage four
steps.text: You receive a costed set of recommendations—what to cut, consolidate, renegotiate or leave alone—plus a dated renewal calendar so the next cycle is planned rather than reactive.
steps.title: Recommendations and renewal calendar

method.heading: How it works
method.lede: Four stages across roughly three weeks. Most of the work happens away from your team—you are needed for a kickoff, a handful of short interviews and the readout.

steps.label: Stage one
steps.text: We collect every tool in use across the practice, including the ones bought on a card and never registered centrally. Each entry gets an owner, a purpose and a dependency.

steps.label: Stage two
steps.text: Short conversations with the people who actually use the stack. What they reach for, what they avoid, and what they have quietly built a workaround around.

steps.label: Stage three
steps.text: We map where two tools do one job, where one tool does none, and where a dependency sits with a single person. Findings are checked against independent product research rather than vendor claims.

items.name: Competition and Visualisation-Led Practice
items.note: xFigura and D5 Render are both image tools, but they sit at different stages. xFigura is for AI concept imagery before the design is fixed, and D5 Render is for production renders from the finished model. In a workflow that sells on imagery, that split is the point of the workflow.
items.short: Image making from the first day, through to jury-ready images, diagrams and film.

stages.does: Supplies a 3D urban context model of the site, so massing and views sit in their real surroundings from the start.
Turns sketches and prompts into concept images on one canvas, so several design directions can be tested before anyone models.
Builds the competition massing and form, with Grasshopper available for parametric options.
Produces the hero images and fly-through from the design model in real time.

items.summary: For practices that win work on imagery, through open and invited competitions or developer pitches. The workflow puts image making at the start, so the team tests ideas visually from the first day and finishes with jury-ready images, diagrams and film.

items.name: Existing Buildings and Retrofit
items.short: From survey to a whole life carbon case, starting from a building that already stands.

stages.does: Scans the existing building on a phone or tablet, with processing on the device and no cloud upload.
Converts the scan into a building model and keeps that model maintained as the building changes.
Compares retrofit options against demolition and new build on whole life carbon.

items.summary: For practices working on refurbishment, adaptive reuse and retrofit, where the starting point is a building that already stands. The workflow goes from survey to a carbon case, because whole life carbon is often the argument that keeps the building standing.

items.name: Residential Design
items.short: Layouts, client visuals and the material choices that decide residential sign-off.

stages.does: Captures the existing house or plot with a phone LiDAR scan, which is enough for extensions and small schemes.
Floor plan options from the brief and site constraints, so the client sees choices early.
Shows material and finish options on the same view, so clients can compare and decide.

items.summary: For practices designing homes, from extensions and new houses to small residential schemes. The workflow balances layout efficiency with the client visuals and material choices that usually decide residential sign-off.

items.name: Early Stage Design I: Feasibility and Site Appraisal
items.short: What a site can take, as tested options with capacity, performance and early carbon.

stages.does: Runs wind, sun and comfort simulations on the site using AI models, in minutes rather than days.
Generates and compares development scenarios, with yield and return figures for each.

items.summary: For the period before a scheme exists, when a client needs to know what a site can take and whether it stacks up. The output is a small set of tested options, each with capacity, environmental performance and early carbon attached.

items.name: Early Stage Design II: Concept to Planning
items.short: One chosen option, developed, explained and checked against policy for planning.

stages.does: Turns sketches and spatial diagrams into editable floor plans and BIM-compatible massing.
Develops the scheme in a collaborative browser-based BIM tool through to planning drawings.
Produces planning-quality CGI from the model in the browser in minutes.

items.summary: Picks up once a feasibility option has been chosen and carries it through to a planning submission. The emphasis moves from testing options to developing one scheme, explaining it well and checking it against policy.

items.name: BIM-Enabled Practice
items.short: Coordinated models through RIBA Stages 3 to 5, built around Revit.

stages.does: Searches the practice’s own models, families and past projects, so teams reuse work instead of redrawing it.
Automates repetitive drawing tasks inside Revit from plain English instructions.
Moves model data between Revit, Rhino and other tools without repeated file exports.

items.summary: For practices delivering coordinated models through RIBA Stages 3 to 5. Revit is not on the list, but several of the tools on it are Revit plugins, so this workflow assumes the practice already authors in Revit and builds around it.

items.name: Bidding Workflow
items.short: Less time finding past work and reading tender packs, more on the proposal.

stages.does: Keeps project sheets, CVs and standard text in a searchable firm intranet, so bid teams find past work quickly.
Turns long tender packs into structured requirements the team can check off.
Produces photorealistic images in seconds from a quick model or sketch, which is enough for most bid responses.

items.summary: For winning appointments through bids, tenders and RFP responses. The workflow cuts the time spent finding past work and reading tender packs, so more of the bid effort goes into the proposal itself.

items.name: Compliance Workflow
items.short: Compliance shown while designing, with records that support the golden thread.

stages.does: Reads UK regulations, technical documents and case law, and connects the rules that apply to the project so gaps show up during design.
Generates construction inspection reports from site observations.

items.summary: For practices that need to show compliance while they design rather than just before issue. For higher-risk buildings, the same records support the golden thread required under the Building Safety Act.

items.name: New Practice
items.short: A complete, low-cost working stack the design team can set up itself.

stages.does: Tracks fees, budgets and time from the first project, which is where new practices most often lose money.
Handles quick 3D design and client models with a short learning curve.
Starts a searchable library of the practice’s own details from day one, so it grows with the practice.

items.summary: For a practice setting up from scratch, or a small practice without a BIM manager, that needs a complete working stack at low cost. Every tool here can be set up by the people doing the design work.

items.name: Workplace and Interiors
items.short: From an existing floor plate to test fits, a chosen plan and sign-off.

stages.does: Captures the existing floor plate as a 3D digital twin, so the fit-out starts from what is actually there.
Generates several workplace layouts from an uploaded PDF or DWG floor plan, ready for the client to compare.
Turns sketches and models into interior renders and short video walkthroughs for client presentations.

items.summary: For practices working on office fit-outs, workplace strategy and interiors, where the job starts from an existing floor plate and the client wants to compare layouts. The workflow moves quickly from test fits to a chosen plan, then to the visuals and product choices the client signs off.

body: ## How it is shaped
Like every partnership, it starts with a call: what you want architects to understand about your company, and the format, scope and timing that suit it.
## How it stays independent
Sponsorship is always disclosed. Sponsors do not preview editorial content, and a founder story does not buy inclusion in recommendations, rankings or reviews, or a place in the ADDD Stack.
items.lede: A founder story introduces your company, and the people behind it, to the architects and practice leaders who follow ADDD.

body: ## How an episode is made
Every episode starts from a piece of architectural work, not from a product. The project is chosen with you and the practice involved, and needs a clear design or delivery problem worth explaining.

The architects and specialists who carried out the work explain their roles and decisions. The workflow is traced step by step: the inputs, the tools at each stage and how information moved between them. Only then does the episode turn to the role your technology played, what it was used for and why it suited the task.
## What is produced
An 8–10 minute workflow video, with a LinkedIn post, a newsletter inclusion, an Instagram Reel and a YouTube Short drawn from it, distributed through ADDD’s channels.
## What it needs from you
A real project or workflow, and a practice willing to take part. The sponsorship is disclosed in the episode itself.
items.lede: One episode built around a real architectural project or workflow: the people who did the work, how they did it, and where your technology fitted into it.

body: ## Where the insight comes from

ADDD works with practices on their technology decisions: reviewing workflows, untangling software estates and helping decide what to adopt, keep or replace. That work shows the problems, constraints and priorities behind their choices, which rarely appear in surveys or sales conversations.
## What a briefing covers

Each quarter’s briefing sets out what practices in your market category are doing, against a scope agreed at the start. It is measured by that scope and its regular delivery, not by conversion figures.
## How confidentiality is kept
Findings are anonymised. No practice is identified, and no raw data is shared.
items.lede: An ongoing intelligence relationship: every quarter, a briefing on what architecture practices in your category are doing, drawn from ADDD’s workshops and sessions with them.

body: ## When it fits

A newsletter placement suits a single, clear message, such as a launch, a useful resource or an event, rather than an ongoing presence. It reaches the architects and practice leaders who read ADDDitive alongside ADDD’s own writing on technology in practice.
## How it is handled
The placement is agreed on a first call: what it says, which issue it runs in and how it is linked. It is marked as a sponsored placement in the issue.

body: ## Choosing the project

Before the session, a short questionnaire helps you choose a project that exposed workflow problems or delays: one where deadlines slipped, information had to be chased or work was done twice. You also receive guidance on who should attend and how to prepare.

A good choice is recent enough that people remember it clearly and broad enough to have passed through several teams and tools. It does not need to be a troubled project, only a typical one: the patterns it shows are the ones every project shares.
## In the room

In the room, the project becomes a shared reference point. Rather than discussing workflows in the abstract, the team walks through what really happened, step by step, with the people who did the work.

Working from one project keeps the session concrete. Each stage is checked against what the project actually produced, the drawings, models, emails and meeting notes, so gaps show up as facts rather than opinions. Where people remember a stage differently, the difference itself is often the finding.
## What it gives you

Because every observation is tied to something the team can point at, the findings are hard to dismiss and easy to act on. The project also becomes a baseline: it can be revisited after changes are made, to see what has improved.
documents.lede: The workshop starts from a project your team has just delivered or is working on now. Because the evidence is your own, the findings describe how your practice actually works, not how a template says it should.
points: Findings grounded in your own work, not general advice
A shared reference everyone in the room recognises
Problems named precisely enough to act on
Evidence drawn from what the project actually produced

body: ## Seeing it all at once

Most practices already sense these problems; they rarely see them all at once, in context, or understand why they keep returning. The session separates symptoms from causes, so the conversation moves from frustration to specifics.
## Tracing the causes

Each friction point is traced back to where it starts: a missing standard, an unclear owner, a tool that does not pass information to the next, or a step that survives only out of habit. Small, frequent losses are counted alongside the visible crises, because together they usually cost the most.

Where it helps, the time involved is estimated with the team: how often a problem occurs, how long it takes each time and who it affects. Rough numbers are enough to show which issues are worth solving first.
## Agreeing what matters

The friction points are then prioritised together, so the team agrees which matter most before anything changes. The written report that follows within two weeks sets them out with practical recommendations and next steps.
documents.lede: With the project laid out, the workshop pinpoints where time is lost: the duplicated effort, the information that disappears between stages, the decisions nobody recorded and the responsibilities that blur.
points: A prioritised list of friction points, agreed by the team
The causes behind recurring delays, not just the symptoms
A clear starting point for change, without a larger commitment
Small, everyday losses counted alongside the visible ones

body: ## Drawing the flow

Mapping the actual flow shows where the handoffs are, which tools each stage depends on and where the same information is entered more than once. It makes the unseen parts of the process visible to everyone at the same time.

The map is drawn live, stage by stage: who does what, with which tools, and what passes to the next person. Loops, workarounds and waiting time are marked where they happen, so the team can see at a glance where the flow slows down or breaks.
## What the map reveals

Seen whole, the flow usually shows a few places where most of the trouble gathers: a stage that waits on another, a tool only one person fully understands, or an approval that holds everything up. These become the focus of the recommendations.
## Using it afterwards
The map becomes a shared picture the whole team can return to. It is the foundation for the findings, priorities and recommendations in the report, and a reference for any change that follows.
documents.lede: Over four hours, the team traces how information, decisions and work move through the practice, from brief to completion, and draws the flow as it really is, not as the process documents describe it.
